a: the earth
p: Erets means both. Here it is the whole world, but Judah's land shows through.
b: The Hebrew 'erets can mean the whole earth or one land, and the KJV switches between them in this chapter ("the land" in 24:3, 11, 13). The chapter speaks of "the world" (tevel, 24:4), of "the peoples" (24:13) and of the army of heaven (24:21), so most translations read "the earth" throughout. Yet the sins named are Israel's: broken laws, a covenant, a city, wine and festivals. The writer seems to take Judah's judgment and widen it to the whole world. The word comes sixteen times in 24:1–20, like a drumbeat.

a: empty the earth and strip it bare
p: Boqeq and boleqah: the words sound like a jug being poured out.
b: The two verbs boqeq ("empty out") and boleqah ("lay waste") rhyme, and they may imitate the gurgle of a jar being poured out (Jeremiah 19:1–7 plays on baqbuq, "jar," and baqqoti, "I will empty"). Nahum 2:10 uses the same sound play for Nineveh. Chapter 24 is full of such paired sounds (24:3, 4, 16, 17, 19), so the poem is meant to be heard aloud.

a: People and priest will fare alike
t: No one is spared by rank
p: Six pairs of opposites: religion, household, market and money all fall together.
b: The list runs through six pairs: the people and the priest, the servant and the master, the maid and the mistress, the buyer and the seller, the lender and the borrower, the creditor and the debtor. Every rank that protects someone in normal times fails. Hosea 4:9 has the same opening, "like people, like priest," for a corrupt priesthood. Here the point is wider: the judgment flattens the whole social order (compare 3:1–7).

a: The earth mourns and wilts
p: Avel means both "mourn" and "dry up." The earth grieves by withering.
b: Hebrew has two verbs spelled 'aval: one means "mourn," the other "dry up" (Amos 1:2). Prophets play on both. When the land "mourns," it withers, and its people's sin is the cause (Hosea 4:1–3; Jeremiah 12:4). The last line, "the lofty among the earth's people," is odd in Hebrew (merom 'am-ha'arets). Some scholars change one vowel to read "the height (heaven) fades along with the earth" (merom 'im ha'arets), and a few modern versions follow them. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: is polluted
p: The word is used for land soaked in innocent blood.
b: Chanefah means "is polluted" or "made godless." The law uses it for blood shed on the land: "Do not pollute the land you live in. Blood pollutes the land" (Numbers 35:33). Jeremiah uses it for a land defiled by unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 3:1–2), and Psalm 106:38 for child sacrifice. The earth is not a neutral stage. What humans do to each other stains it.

a: the everlasting covenant
p: Noah's covenant with all life, Sinai, or a law written into creation?
b: The whole world has broken "the everlasting covenant" (berit 'olam). Israel's covenant at Sinai fits the words "laws" and "rule," but the nations never received it. So many scholars think of God's covenant with Noah and "every living creature" (Genesis 9:16, the same phrase), with its ban on bloodshed (Genesis 9:5–6), which matches "polluted" (see above). Others read a broad covenant of creation, a moral order every people knows (Romans 1:18–21; 2:14–15). Some think the writer simply applies Israel's covenant language to everyone. The flood imagery of 24:18 supports the Noah reading.

a: a curse is eating the earth
p: 'Alah is the curse sworn when a covenant is made, which falls when it is broken.
b: An 'alah is the curse a person accepts on oath when making a covenant: if I break it, may this happen to me. Deuteronomy warns that every curse "written in this book" will settle on the one who breaks the covenant (Deuteronomy 29:20–21), and Daniel 9:11 says the curse "has been poured out" on Israel. Zechariah 5:3 pictures the curse flying over the whole land. Here it "eats" the earth like fire, and the people "burn away."

a: The new wine mourns
p: 24:7–12 strip away wine, music and song. 25:6 gives them back on God's mountain.
b: These verses picture a city whose parties have stopped: no new wine, no tambourines, no lyre, no songs at the cup, only people crying in the streets over wine that is gone. Wine in the Bible is a sign of blessing and joy (Psalm 104:15), so its loss means God's blessing has left. The pattern will be reversed in 25:6, where the LORD himself spreads a feast with the finest wine for all peoples. Israel's prophets often pair the two scenes (Joel 1:5, 10–12; 3:18; Amos 9:13–14).

a: beer
p: Shekar was mostly beer made from grain, not distilled liquor.
b: Shekar is rendered "beer" on this site. In the ancient Near East it was mostly beer brewed from barley, and perhaps other fermented drinks such as date wine. Distilling had not yet been invented, so "strong drink" (KJV) can mislead a modern reader. The word comes again in 28:7 and 29:9.

a: The city of chaos
p: Unnamed on purpose? Babylon, Moab's capital, Samaria, Jerusalem and Tyre have all been proposed.
b: The city is never named, here or in 25:2, 26:5 and 27:10. Its title, qiryat tohu, uses the word for the "shapeless" earth of Genesis 1:2 (Plain English Translation "shapeless"): the city is sliding back into chaos. Proposals include Babylon, destroyed by Sennacherib in 689 BC or taken by Cyrus in 539; a Moabite city, because Moab is named in 25:10; Samaria (722) or Jerusalem (587); and Tyre, the subject of chapter 23. Many scholars now think the namelessness is the point: the "city of chaos" stands for every proud human city set against God, as Babylon does in Revelation 17–18.

a: has gone into exile
p: Galah is the verb for a people carried into exile.
b: The word galah usually describes people deported from their land (5:13; 2 Kings 17:6; 25:21). Here the earth's gladness is the captive led away. For first readers who knew Assyria's and Babylon's deportations, the image was concrete: whole towns marched away in lines, leaving fields and vineyards silent.

a: like the beating of an olive tree
t: A few olives left on the branch
p: Harvest leftovers: a picture of the remnant. 17:6 used it for Israel.
b: Olives were harvested by beating the branches with a stick, and grapes by picking the clusters. A few always stayed behind, and the law left them for the poor (Deuteronomy 24:20–21). Isaiah 17:6 used the same picture for the few who would be left in Israel, and here it is widened to the peoples of the earth. The picture is bleak, but it leaves room for survivors, and the next verse hears them singing.

a: from the sea they cry aloud
p: "From the sea" means from the west. The singers are not named.
b: Miyyam, "from the sea," is the usual Hebrew way to say "from the west," since the Mediterranean lay west of Israel. The Hebrew begins with an emphatic "they" (hemmah): the survivors of 24:13, scattered to the coasts and islands, or Jews of the dispersion, or the nations themselves. The joy is surprising in the middle of judgment, and the prophet's own response in 24:16 is to say it is too early to sing. The Greek reads quite differently: "those who are left on the land will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord."

a: in the lands of the dawn
p: Ba'urim means "in the lights." Most take it as the region of the sunrise.
b: Ba'urim literally means "in the lights" or "in the fires" (KJV "in the fires"). Because it stands opposite "the far shores of the sea" (the west), most interpreters take it as the lands of light, the east, where the sun rises. Others suggest a small change to be'iyyim, "in the coastlands," making the line repeat the next one, and the Greek has no word for it at all. Either way the call is for praise from both ends of the world.

a: Splendor to the Righteous One!
p: Tsaddiq without a name: the LORD, or the righteous who survive.
b: Tsevi latsaddiq means "splendor (glory, beauty) to the righteous one." Many take the Righteous One as God, praised by the far-off singers. Others read "the righteous" as a group: glory belongs to the faithful who survive (KJV "glory to the righteous"). The Greek turns the line into "hope for the godly." The title "the Righteous One" is later used of the Messiah (1 Enoch 38:2; Acts 3:14; 7:52).

a: I grow thin, I grow thin!
p: Razi li: wasting away, or, read as Aramaic, "My secret is mine."
b: The rare word razi comes from razah, "become thin" (17:4), so the prophet cries that he is wasting away with grief, as in the KJV's "My leanness." But raz is also the Aramaic word for a "mystery" (Daniel 2:18–19), and Jerome's Latin reads secretum meum mihi, "My secret is mine, my secret is mine." The Targum also hears a revealed mystery here. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew sense. Either way the prophet cannot join the singing: he sees the betrayal that still has to be judged.

a: Double-crossers double-cross!
p: Bogdim bagadu u-veged bogdim bagadu: the betrayal is said five times.
b: The line repeats the root b-g-d, "betray, deal faithlessly," five times in six words: bogdim bagadu u-veged bogdim bagadu. The Plain English Translation keeps the pile-up and uses "double-cross," as in 21:2, where the same phrase appears; and the woe of 33:1 turns it against the destroyer. The word is used of a faithless spouse (Jeremiah 3:20; Malachi 2:14) and a treaty partner who breaks faith.

a: Terror, trench and trap
p: Three words that sound alike, and each one catches whoever escapes the one before.
b: Hebrew pachad wafachat wafach is a tongue-twister: terror, pit, snare. The Plain English Translation keeps the sound with "terror, trench and trap." Verse 18 explains: whoever runs from the noise falls into the pit, and whoever climbs out is caught in the trap. Amos 5:19 has the same kind of chain (the lion, the bear, the snake), and Jeremiah 48:43–44 reuses these very words for Moab.

a: the windows high above have been opened
p: The same windows opened at Noah's flood (Genesis 7:11) open again.
b: In Genesis "the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11) to send the flood, and they "were shut" again (Genesis 8:2). Isaiah uses the same word (arubbot). With "the everlasting covenant" of 24:5 broken, creation seems to run backward: the waters return and the earth's foundations shake. Later in Isaiah God promises that this will not happen to Zion again: "as I swore that Noah's waters would never again sweep over the earth" (54:9).

a: like a shack in a field
p: A flimsy shelter put up for the harvest season, then left to blow over.
b: The melunah was a hut of branches put up in a cucumber or melon field for a watchman at harvest time (1:8). It was meant for a season and then abandoned to the wind. The earth itself, once "set firm" so that "it will not totter" (Psalm 93:1), now sways like a drunk and like such a shack.

a: the army on high, up on high
p: The "army of the height" may be stars, gods of the nations, or angels who rebelled.
b: Tseva hammarom, "the army of the height," is set beside "the kings of the earth." The "army of heaven" can mean the stars (40:26) or heavenly beings around God's throne (1 Kings 22:19). Here they are judged, so most readers think of heavenly powers that stand behind earthly kings: the gods of the nations (Deuteronomy 4:19; Psalm 82), the princes of Persia and Greece in Daniel 10:13 and 10:20, or angels who rebelled. 1 Enoch 10 and 18–21 tell of angels bound in a pit until the day of judgment, and 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 echo that tradition. Revelation 20:1–3 binds Satan in the abyss in a similar way.
r: Deuteronomy 4:19; Psalm 82:1–7; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20; 1 Enoch 10:4–6; 1 Enoch 18:13–16; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6; Revelation 20:1–3

a: they will be called to account
p: Paqad can mean "punish" or "attend to." After many days, something happens to the prisoners.
b: The verb paqad means to attend to, inspect or call to account. In 24:21 it plainly means punishment, and the Plain English Translation uses the same English here, as the Hebrew uses the same verb. But yippaqedu could also mean "they will be visited" (KJV) in the sense of "dealt with" or even "released," as in a prisoner's case finally being heard. Two stages are pictured: first a prison, then, "after many days," a final reckoning. Readers of 1 Enoch saw the binding of the Watchers here, and many premillennial readers see the thousand years of Revelation 20, with Satan bound and then released "for a short time" (Revelation 20:3, 7–10).

a: The pale moon will blush
p: Isaiah uses poetic names for the moon and sun, perhaps to avoid their divine names.
b: The usual words for moon and sun are yareach and shemesh, which were also names of gods. Here Isaiah uses the poetic levanah, "the white one," and chammah, "the hot one" (also in 30:26 and Song of Songs 6:10). The lights people worshiped are put to shame when the true King appears. The Greek read the same letters as other words; see the variant.

a: the LORD of Armies will be king on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem
p: Malakh YHWH: the cry of the kingship psalms, here as the end of history.
b: Malakh YHWH, "the LORD reigns" or "the LORD has become king," is the cry of the kingship psalms: "The LORD is King!" (Psalm 93:1; 97:1; 99:1). Here it is the climax of the world's judgment: after the earth's kings and the powers on high are dealt with, God's own rule is set up on Zion. The Targum says "the kingdom of the LORD of hosts will be revealed" on Mount Zion (Chilton; some older English renderings have "power" or "might"), and Chilton ties it to the feast of 25:6 and to Jesus' words about many sitting at table in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11; Luke 13:28–29). Revelation hears the same hope: "The kingdom of the world ... has become our Lord's and his Messiah's" (Revelation 11:15).
r: Psalm 93:1; Psalm 97:1; Psalm 99:1; 52:7; Micah 4:7; Revelation 11:15; Revelation 19:6; Matthew 8:11; Luke 13:28–29

a: before his elders there will be glory
p: Like the seventy elders on Sinai, who saw God and ate before him.
b: The elders recall Exodus 24:9–11, where Moses, Aaron and seventy elders of Israel went up the mountain: "They saw the God of Israel," and "they looked upon God, and they ate and drank" (Exodus 24:10–11). Isaiah moves the scene to Zion, and the next chapter opens with a feast on "this mountain" (25:6). Revelation's twenty-four elders around the throne (Revelation 4:4) continue the picture.

a: truth that holds firm
p: 'Emunah 'omen: two words from the root that gives us "amen."
b: The line ends with 'emunah 'omen, two nouns from the root '-m-n, "be firm, be reliable," the root of "amen" and of he'emin, "believe" (7:9; 28:16). God's plans are as solid as their source. The KJV's "faithfulness and truth" gives both words; many modern versions merge them into one phrase.

a: plans laid from long ago
p: God's "wonder" and "plans" return in 28:29, and in the child's name in 9:6.
b: Isaiah often insists that what happens in history was planned by God long before (22:11; 37:26; 46:10). The words pele' ("wonder") and 'etsot ("plans, counsel") come together again in 28:29, and in the throne name "Wonderful Counselor" (9:6, pele' yo'ets). The song praises God for the fall of the city in 25:2 as the result of a long-laid plan.

a: The palace of outsiders
p: Zar is someone who does not belong: here foreign conquerors.
b: Zarim are "outsiders," people who do not belong to a family, a priesthood or a people. In Isaiah the word means foreigners who invade and occupy (1:7; 29:5; 61:5). The Plain English Translation renders it "outsiders" throughout, as elsewhere on the site, and keeps nokhri for "foreigner." The fallen city again has no name (see 24:10). The Greek has "the ungodly," and some scholars read zedim, "the arrogant," which differs by one letter.

a: a strong people will honor you
t: Enemies who learn to fear God
p: The brutal nations themselves end up giving God honor.
b: The city's fall leads "a strong people" and "the city of brutal nations" to honor and fear the LORD. Some read this as the conversion of the nations, as in 19:21–25, where Egypt and Assyria worship the LORD. Others read it as the forced respect of defeated enemies. Either way, the song says the judgment has a purpose beyond destruction: the world comes to know who God is.

a: beating on a wall
t: A storm against a wall, or a winter storm?
p: Qir is "wall"; one vowel change gives qor, "cold."
b: The Hebrew says the blast of the brutal is "like a downpour (against) a wall" (kezerem qir). Many scholars read qor, "cold," making it "a winter rainstorm," which fits the pairing with "heat" in 25:5. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. The picture is the same either way: God is a shelter in storm and shade in heat for the poor (compare 4:6; 32:2).

a: a fortress for the poor
p: The fall of the brutal city is good news for the poor and needy.
b: The poor (dal) and the needy ('evyon) are those the brutal ('aritsim) push around. Isaiah's earlier oracles condemned Judah's leaders for crushing the poor (3:14–15; 10:1–2), and the Psalms call God their stronghold (Psalm 9:9; Psalm 14:6). Here God himself becomes the poor man's fortress (ma'oz). The same word comes in 27:5 and in 30:2–3, where Judah chooses "Pharaoh's fortress" instead.

a: a feast for all the peoples
p: God's banquet for every nation: messianic banquet, Lord's Supper, or a feast of judgment?
b: On "this mountain," Zion, the LORD spreads a feast for "all the peoples," like the meal the elders ate before God on Sinai (Exodus 24:11; see Isaiah 24:23). Jewish tradition developed it into the banquet of the age to come, sometimes with Leviathan as the main dish (2 Baruch 29:4; Bavli Bava Batra 74b–75a), and Jesus spoke of many coming "from the sunrise and the sunset" to "eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 8:11). Revelation calls it "the wedding supper of the Lamb" (Revelation 19:9), and many Christians see a foretaste in the Lord's Supper. The Targum reverses the scene: the nations expect a feast of glory but receive shame and plagues they cannot escape.
r: Exodus 24:11; 24:23; 55:1–2; Matthew 8:11; Luke 13:29; Luke 14:15; Revelation 19:9; 2 Baruch 29:4–8

a: wine aged on its dregs
t: Fat foods and wine on the lees
p: Shemanim and shemarim: rich food and wine left to mature on its sediment.
b: Shemanim are "fat things," the richest food, and shemarim are "dregs": wine left to stand on its sediment so that it gains strength and flavor, then strained clear (mezuqqaqim, "refined"). The two words sound alike and are each said twice. Elsewhere, wine on its dregs is a picture of complacency (Jeremiah 48:11; Zephaniah 1:12), but here it is simply the best wine there is. The Greek turns the line into "they will drink joy, they will drink wine, they will anoint themselves with myrrh."

a: the shroud that lies over all the peoples
p: A cloth over the face: grief, shame and death. God swallows it up.
b: Mourners covered their heads and faces (2 Samuel 15:30; 2 Samuel 19:4; Jeremiah 14:3–4), and the dead were wrapped for burial. The "shroud" (lot) and "woven sheet" (massekhah) over every nation are the grief and death that hang over all humanity. God "swallows" them, the same verb used for death in the next verse. Paul's image of a veil over the heart that is taken away in Christ (2 Corinthians 3:14–16) is often read beside this verse.

a: He will swallow death up for all time
p: Paul quotes it at 1 Corinthians 15:54, in a Greek form close to Theodotion's.
b: Death, which "swallows" everyone (Proverbs 1:12; Habakkuk 2:5), is itself swallowed by God. Paul ends his chapter on the resurrection with this verse: "Death has been swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54). His wording is not the usual Greek of Isaiah, which says "Death, having prevailed, swallowed them up" (see the variant), but matches the later Greek version of Theodotion. Paul's "in victory" renders lanetsach, "forever," in a sense the word has in Aramaic and later Hebrew, "victory." The Mishnah ends a tractate on mourning with this verse as the hope that mourning will end (Mishnah Moed Katan 3:9).

a: swallow death
p: In the Baal myth Death has a huge mouth that swallows the gods. Here God swallows Death.
b: In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle (tablets written about 1300–1200 BC), Death (Mot) is a god whose throat reaches from earth to sky, and he swallows Baal (KTU 1.5 ii 2–6). Habakkuk 2:5 and Proverbs 1:12 still speak of death's open throat. Isaiah turns the picture around: the LORD swallows Death. Most scholars think the image draws on this old Canaanite language, and Isaiah uses it to say the opposite of the myth. In the myth Baal comes back only for a season, while here death ends for good.

a: The Lord GOD will wipe the tears off every face
p: Revelation quotes it twice, for the martyrs and for the new creation.
b: Revelation uses the line twice: for the crowd before the throne, "God will wipe every tear from their eyes" (Revelation 7:17), and for the new creation: "He will wipe every tear out of their eyes. Death will be gone, and grief and crying and pain will be gone too" (Revelation 21:4). Isaiah's "every face" is not limited to Israel: the feast and the comfort are for "all the peoples" (25:6–7). Isaiah 65:19 repeats the promise: no more weeping in Jerusalem.

a: the scorn his people bear
p: The nations' contempt for Israel ends.
b: Cherpah is public scorn, the shame of defeat, exile or childlessness (4:1; 54:4). Israel had been mocked among the nations for its God's apparent weakness (Psalm 79:4; Ezekiel 36:20–21). The universal feast still has a particular note: God's own people are vindicated before everyone.

a: We hoped in him
p: Qavah means to wait with expectation, like a stretched cord.
b: Qivvinu, "we waited, we hoped," comes twice. The verb qavah is related to qav, a measuring line or cord (28:17), and is often explained as "stretch toward." It is the waiting of 40:31 and Psalm 130:5. The song is the joy of people whose long waiting has been answered: "Here he is, our God!" (compare 40:9).

a: Moab will be trodden down
p: In the middle of a world-wide feast, one neighbor is named for judgment.
b: After the feast for "all the peoples," Moab alone is trodden down like straw in manure. Moab had a long history of conflict with Israel (Numbers 22–25; 2 Kings 3), and Isaiah had already given it two chapters (15–16; compare Jeremiah 48; Zephaniah 2:8–11). Many scholars think Moab stands for the proud nations as a group, as Edom does in 34:5–6 and 63:1–6, because pride (25:11) is the sin named. Others think of a real grievance of the writer's day, perhaps Moab's gloating over Jerusalem's fall (Ezekiel 25:8–11).

a: a manure pit
p: The word for dung pit sounds like Madmen, a town of Moab.
b: Madmenah means a dung heap or manure pit, where straw was trodden into the muck to make fertilizer. Jeremiah 48:2 names a Moabite town Madmen, and the sound play here may be deliberate. The Ketiv and the Great Isaiah Scroll say "in the water of" the manure pit (see the variant), which leads into the picture of swimming in 25:11.

a: as a swimmer spreads out his hands
p: Moab flailing in the muck, or the LORD pressing it down?
b: The Hebrew says only "he will spread out his hands in it." Most interpreters take "he" as Moab, flailing like a swimmer in the manure pit, while God brings its pride down. Some medieval and modern readers take "he" as the LORD, who stretches out his hands to push Moab under, as a swimmer pushes the water down. The last line, "for all the tricks of its hands," may mean "in spite of" Moab's skill, or "together with" its schemes.

a: Ours is a city of strength!
p: The strong city of God's people answers the fallen "city of chaos."
b: Chapters 24–27 set two cities against each other. The "city of chaos" is broken (24:10), the fortified city of outsiders becomes rubble (25:2), and the town set high is knocked to the dust (26:5). Over against them stands "a city of strength" whose walls are God's rescue (yeshu'ah), not stone. Revelation draws the same contrast between fallen Babylon and the new Jerusalem (Revelation 18; 21), and Augustine built his City of God on two cities, the earthly and the heavenly.

a: Open the gates
p: Like the Temple entrance psalms, the song asks who may come in.
b: The call to open the gates recalls the entrance liturgies of the Psalms: "Open the gates of righteousness for me" (Psalm 118:19) and "Gates, lift your heads high!" (Psalm 24:7). There the righteous or the King of glory enters; here "a righteous nation" comes in, one that "stays true" (shomer 'emunim, "keeps faithfulness"). The question of who may enter God's city returns in 33:14–16 and in Psalm 15.

a: you guard in peace, peace
p: Hebrew doubles a word for completeness: "peace, peace" is peace in full.
b: The verse is compact: yetser samukh titstsor shalom shalom, literally "a mind propped up you keep, peace, peace." Yetser is the shaping of thought, the inner inclination (Genesis 8:21), and samukh means "leaning on, supported." The Hebrew has no "on you" after samukh; the KJV's "stayed on thee" supplies it from the last clause, and the Plain English Translation does not. Doubling a word is Hebrew's way of saying "complete," hence the KJV's "perfect peace." The same doubling comes in 57:19: "Peace, peace, to the one who is far and the one who is near" (57:19). The verb natsar, "guard," may also echo yetser in sound.

a: Yah, the LORD
t: Yah YHWH and the everlasting rock
p: Yah is the short form of God's name, heard in "Hallelu-yah."
b: Yah is the short form of the divine name, as in "Hallelujah" and in Exodus 15:2 and Isaiah 12:2, where the same doubled form "Yah YHWH" occurs. God is a tsur 'olamim, "a rock of ages," the KJV margin's "rock of ages," from which Augustus Toplady's hymn takes its name. Rock is an old title for God as refuge (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 18:2), and it returns in this part at 30:29, "the Rock of Israel."

a: he knocks it down to the dust
p: The verbs of 25:12 return, and the poor now walk on the ruins.
b: The chain of verbs is the one used against Moab's walls in 25:12: "bring down," "lay low," "knock to the ground," "to the dust." The Plain English Translation keeps the wording close in both places so that the echo can be heard. In 26:6 the reversal is complete: the town set high is trodden by "the feet of the afflicted." The poor, who were crushed, now walk over the ruins of the proud (compare 2:11–17; 1 Samuel 2:8).

a: you level the track of the righteous
t: The Upright One, or an upright road?
p: Yashar may be a title for God or simply describe the path.
b: The second line begins with yashar, "upright, straight." It can be read as a title addressed to God, "Upright One, you level the track of the righteous," as the KJV and many modern versions take it, or as a description of the path: "you make the track of the righteous level and straight," as the Plain English Translation does. The verb pillas, "make level," comes again in 40:3–4, where every valley is lifted and the road is made straight.

a: I crave you through the night
p: The night watch of prayer: the soul searches for God until morning.
b: The singer's longing runs from night to dawn: "my whole being" (nafshi) and "my spirit" (ruchi) seek God. The Psalms speak the same way: "My soul is thirsty for you; my body aches for you" (Psalm 63:1), "Through the watches of the night I murmur about you" (Psalm 63:6). In a book that often speaks of night as danger (21:11–12), night becomes the time of waiting for God's dawn.

a: Show favor to the wicked
p: The world learns from God's judgments, but the wicked do not learn even from kindness.
b: Verses 9–10 set two lessons side by side. When God's judgments reach the earth, people learn righteousness. But favor shown to the wicked teaches them nothing: even in a land of honest dealing they twist things. Some read this as the prophet's call for judgment, since grace has been wasted on the wicked (compare 5:4). Others see a sober observation that kindness alone does not change a hard heart, so God's patience must one day give way to justice (Romans 2:4–5; 2 Peter 3:9). The Greek turns verse 10 into a prayer: "let the ungodly be taken away."

a: your passion for your people
p: Qin'at 'am: God's passionate zeal for his people.
b: Qin'ah is burning, possessive passion: jealousy, zeal or ardor. The phrase qin'at 'am is literally "zeal of a people." Most read it as God's zeal for his people (compare 9:7; 37:32, "the zeal of the LORD of Armies"). A few take it as the people's zeal, or as God's zeal against the nations. The enemies who would not see God's raised hand will see his passion to defend his own and be ashamed.

a: you have worked it for us
p: What Israel achieved was God's doing.
b: "Even all our work you have worked for us" confesses that whatever good the people achieved was God's gift. Christian readers have often cited the line in discussions of grace: the good that believers do is first God's own work in them. Paul says something close: "the one at work in you is God. He works in you both the wanting and the doing" (Philippians 2:13). Verse 18 says the opposite about human effort without God: labor that gives birth only to wind.

a: masters other than you have owned us
p: Be'alunu: "they have been our ba'als"; foreign kings, or other gods.
b: The verb be'alunu means "they have owned us, been lords over us," from ba'al, "owner, master, husband," also the name of the Canaanite god Baal. Some read the line as foreign rulers who governed Israel (Assyria, Babylon, Persia). Others hear a confession of having served other gods. Either way, the confession is of loyalty: "you alone, your name alone, we keep in mind." The Hebrew nazkir, "we call to mind," can also mean "we invoke" in worship.

a: shades do not rise
p: Refa'im: the shadowy dead, and in Ugarit the royal dead ancestors.
b: Refa'im are the "shades," the faint, powerless dead in Sheol (14:9; Psalm 88:10; Proverbs 9:18). At Ugarit the rpum were the deified royal ancestors, called up in rituals. In the Bible the Rephaim are also an ancient race of giants (Deuteronomy 2:11; 3:11). Here the oppressors who once ruled Israel (26:13) are dead and will not rise. In 26:19 the same word comes back: the earth will give birth to "her shades." What is denied to the oppressors is promised to God's own dead.

a: pushed out all the borders of the land
p: Richaqta: "you have made far": borders enlarged, or the people sent far away?
b: The verb richaqta means "you have made far, removed far." Most versions take it as the borders of the land pushed outward, as in Israel's promised growth (Genesis 15:18; 54:2–3). Some read it as "you have removed (the people) far to all the ends of the land," referring to the scattering of exile. The doubled "you have added to the nation" suggests growth, and the Plain English Translation reads it that way.

a: they poured out a murmur
p: Lachash is a whisper, sometimes a charm. Here, prayer reduced to a murmur.
b: The Hebrew is difficult: tsaqun lachash musarkha lamo, roughly "they poured out a whisper, your discipline (was) on them." Lachash is a whisper and also a spell or charm (3:3, 3:20; Jeremiah 8:17). The picture is of people so crushed that they can only murmur their prayers. The word "discipline" (musar) is the correction a father gives a child (Proverbs 3:11–12), so their suffering is read as God's training, not abandonment.

a: As a pregnant woman near her time
p: Birth pains are Isaiah's image for crisis; here the labor bears only wind.
b: Labor pains are a regular biblical picture of terror and crisis (13:8; 21:3; Jeremiah 4:31). At the Assyrian siege Hezekiah would say, "The children have come right to the mouth of the womb, but there is no strength to push them out" (37:3). Here the people's own effort brings forth nothing: "we gave birth to wind." Isaiah 66:7–9 reverses the picture, as Zion gives birth before her pains come. The New Testament uses the image for the pains before the new age (Mark 13:8; John 16:21; Romans 8:22; Revelation 12:2).

a: no people have been born to fill the world
p: Nafal, "fall," can mean "be born"; the next verse plays on it.
b: The Hebrew says, "the inhabitants of the world have not fallen." The verb nafal, "fall," can describe a baby dropping at birth, as in the Aramaic and later Hebrew use of the word, and the parallel with childbirth makes this sense likely. The next verse answers it with the same root in its causative form: the earth "will make fall," that is, give birth to, its shades (26:19). The Greek read it the other way, as defeat: "all the inhabitants of the earth will fall."

a: Your dead will live!
p: Is this the first clear promise of the resurrection of the dead, or a picture of Israel restored?
b: The verse answers 26:14. The oppressors' dead will not rise, but "your dead will live." Many scholars read this as one of the earliest Old Testament statements of personal resurrection, a step toward Daniel 12:2, which uses the same language: "Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up. Some will wake to life without end." Others, noting the national laments around it, read it like Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:1–14): the near-dead nation will rise again. The two need not exclude each other, since a hope for the nation could ground a hope for the dead. Rabban Gamaliel cites the verse as proof of resurrection from the Prophets (Bavli Sanhedrin 90b), and the Targum renders it "you revive the dead." The earliest translation already heard bodily resurrection: the Old Greek reads "the dead will rise, and those in the tombs will be raised," adding the word "tombs."
r: 26:14; Daniel 12:2; Ezekiel 37:1–14; Hosea 6:2; 1 Samuel 2:6; John 11:25; 1 Corinthians 15:52

a: My corpses will rise!
p: Nevelati is singular, "my corpse": God's, the prophet's, or the people's?
b: Nevelati is literally "my corpse," a singular noun used as a collective ("my dead bodies"). If God is the speaker, the dead belong to him: "your dead, my corpses." If the prophet speaks, the dead are his people. The KJV takes it as "together with my dead body shall they arise," the prophet expecting to rise with them, and some Christian readers have heard Christ rising with his people. The Targum softens the term to "the bones of their dead bodies."

a: For your dew is dew that sparkles with light
p: Tal 'orot: dew of lights, or dew of herbs. In Jewish tradition, the dew of resurrection.
b: Tal 'orot may mean "dew of lights," the shining dew of dawn, or "dew of herbs," since 'orot means plants in 2 Kings 4:39. Dew is life-giving moisture in a dry land (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5). Rabbinic tradition speaks of a "dew with which the Holy One will revive the dead" kept in the highest heaven (Bavli Chagigah 12b; Bavli Shabbat 88b), and the daily Amidah praises God "who causes the dew to fall" in the blessing on the resurrection. Rabbi Elazar read "dew of lights" as the light of Torah (Bavli Ketubot 111b). The Greek has "the dew from you is healing for them."

a: the earth will bring her shades to birth
p: Tappil: the earth "lets fall" its dead, as a mother delivers a child.
b: The verb tappil is the causative of nafal, "fall": the earth will "make fall" its refa'im, delivering them as a mother delivers a baby. Where the people's labor gave birth to wind (26:18), the earth's labor brings forth the dead. The shades denied resurrection in 26:14 are the oppressors; here they are God's people. The Greek reads it as judgment: "the land of the ungodly will fall."

a: go into your inner rooms
t: Shut in until the anger passes
p: Like Noah in the ark and Israel on Passover night, God's people are told to shut the door.
b: The command recalls two rescues. Noah went into the ark, and "the LORD shut the door behind him" (Genesis 7:16). On Passover night no one was to "go out the door of his house until morning" while the LORD passed through (Exodus 12:22–23). Here God's people hide "for just a moment" until the fury has passed (compare 54:7–8). Jesus' words on prayer use the same picture: "go into the storeroom of your house and close the door behind you" (Matthew 6:6).

a: The earth will lay bare its blood
t: The ground gives up its dead
p: Blood soaked into the ground cries out, as Abel's did.
b: From Abel's murder onward the Bible pictures shed blood crying from the ground: "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Blood "pollutes the land" (Numbers 35:33), which links this verse back to the polluted earth of 24:5. Murder that the earth has hidden will be exposed. The same hope for justice for the slain is heard from the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:9–10.

a: Leviathan the fleeing serpent
t: Leviathan and the Ugaritic Baal texts
p: The same three names appear in Canaanite poems written centuries before Isaiah.
b: Clay tablets from Ugarit (about 1300–1200 BC) contain almost the same words. Death taunts Baal: "When you struck Litan, the fleeing serpent, finished off the twisting serpent, the tyrant with seven heads" (KTU 1.5 i 1–3). The goddess Anat boasts that she muzzled the dragon (tnn) and crushed the twisting serpent (KTU 1.3 iii 38–42). Isaiah's liwyatan, nachash bariach, nachash 'aqallaton and tannin match ltn, btn brh, btn 'qltn and tnn. The borrowing of poetic language is not in doubt; what Isaiah means by it is (see the next note).

a: the dragon that lives in the sea
p: Nations, the power of chaos, or the devil? Each reading has old support.
b: Readers have identified the monster in three main ways. (1) Nations: the Targum makes the beasts kings "like Pharaoh" and "like Sennacherib," and Rashi follows the Targum; the three titles would then be three empires. (2) Chaos and evil: many scholars read the old myth as a picture of every power hostile to God, finally destroyed "on that day," as the sea itself is gone in Revelation 21:1. (3) The devil: Revelation names the dragon as "the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9), and Christian readers have long read 27:1 of his defeat. Some scholars (Tsumura) caution that Israel's use of the language need not carry the myth's theology with it.

a: with his sword, hard and great and strong
p: Bariach and 'aqallaton: a monster that slips away and coils.
b: Bariach probably means "fleeing" (the Greek has pheugonta), a serpent that slips away; others suggest "primeval" or "slippery." 'Aqallaton, "crooked, twisting," is from the same root as the "crooked paths" of Judges 5:6. Job 26:13 uses the first title: "his hand ran through the fleeing snake." Where the Ugaritic gods fight with clubs and nets, here the LORD alone wields his sword, and the verb is paqad, "call to account," as in 24:21: the monster is judged, not merely beaten.

a: A delightful vineyard, sing of it!
p: Chapter 5 sang of a vineyard God would ruin. Here he guards it.
b: Isaiah 5:1–7 was a love song that turned into judgment: the vineyard produced only stinking grapes, and God would let thornbush and bramble overgrow it. This new song answers that one point by point. God keeps it and waters it constantly, guards it night and day, and has no anger left. The thornbush and bramble of 5:6 come back, but now God wants them only to fight them (27:4). The picture of Israel as God's vine runs through the Bible (Psalm 80:8–16; Jeremiah 2:21) to Jesus' "I am the real vine" (John 15:1).

a: I water it moment by moment
p: Lirga'im: "at every moment," the opposite of the withheld rain of 5:6.
b: Lirga'im means "at every moment, constantly." In 5:6 God commanded the clouds not to rain on the vineyard; now he waters it himself without pause. The phrase "so that no one lays a hand on it" uses paqad again, here in the sense "harm, attack." God watching "night and day" recalls Psalm 121:4, where the one who guards Israel "does not doze and does not sleep."

a: There is no fury in me
p: God says he has no wrath left for his vineyard; only its enemies need fear.
b: Chemah 'en li, "wrath I do not have." The fury that hid God's people for a moment in 26:20 has passed. Instead, God wishes for thornbush and bramble to fight. These are the weeds of 5:6 and 7:23–25, which may stand for enemies or for whatever chokes the vineyard. The alternative comes in 27:5: let them make peace with God instead. The Greek translator read the verse very differently, of a city besieged and burned.

a: let him make peace with me
p: Even the thorns may become friends if they take hold of God's fortress.
b: The "him" is the enemy pictured as thorns, or anyone threatening the vineyard. Instead of being burned, he may "take hold of" God's fortress (ma'uzzi), as a fugitive grasped the horns of the altar for asylum (1 Kings 1:50). The doubled "make peace with me" stresses the offer. Some read this of the nations finding refuge in Israel's God (compare 25:3–4; 56:6–7), others of Israelites who had gone astray. The chiastic repetition, "let him make peace with me; peace with me let him make," is kept in the Plain English Translation.

a: they will cover the surface of the world with fruit
p: The vine that gave rotten grapes will fill the whole world with fruit.
b: In 5:2 the vineyard gave only stinking grapes; here Jacob takes root and fills the world (tevel) with fruit. The promise to Abraham that "All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you" (Genesis 12:3) stands in the background. Jewish readers have heard Israel's Torah and witness; Christian readers have heard the spread of the gospel from Israel to the nations (Romans 11:12; John 15:5, 8).

a: Did the LORD strike him down the way he struck down the one who struck him?
p: God punished Israel less harshly than he punished Israel's attackers.
b: The two questions expect the answer "no." Israel was struck, but not destroyed the way its enemies were. Most read "him" as Jacob and "the one who struck him" as the oppressor nation, whose ruin was total (compare 10:12–19; 14:3–23). Some medieval Jewish interpreters read it as a promise to the exiles: Israel's punishment was discipline, while the empires that struck it disappeared. The idea of measured judgment leads into 27:8.

a: With measured blows, by sending her away
p: Sa'se'ah may be "by measure" or a cry to drive animals off. Sending away is divorce language.
b: Bessa'sse'ah is unique. Many link it to se'ah, a grain measure, so that the punishment was given "by measure," in exact proportion (Rashi reads "measure for measure"). Others connect it with a cry used to drive animals away ("shoo!"). "Sending her away" (beshalchah) is the verb for divorce: a husband "sends her away from his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1). Israel, God's wife, was sent into exile but not finally rejected (50:1; 54:6–7). The feminine "her" fits that picture of Zion as wife.

a: this is how Jacob's guilt will be atoned for
p: Paul joins this verse to 59:20–21: "when I take away their sins."
b: The verb kipper, "atone," is rare in the prophets. The Greek renders the second line "and this is his blessing, when I take away his sin," and Paul quotes that wording, joined to 59:20–21, at the climax of his argument about Israel: "And this is the covenant from me for them: when I take away their sins" (Romans 11:27). In Isaiah the sign of forgiveness is practical: Jacob smashes the altars of other gods. Paul applies it to the future salvation of "all Israel" (Romans 11:26).

a: no Asherah poles or incense stands will be left upright
p: Asherim were wooden cult poles; chammanim were small altars, probably for incense.
b: The 'asherim were wooden poles or stylized trees, symbols of the goddess Asherah, who in some inscriptions is named beside the LORD (Kuntillet 'Ajrud, about 800 BC). The chammanim were probably small incense altars (Leviticus 26:30, "I will... cut down your incense stands"); older versions guessed "sun images." Grinding altar stones "like lumps of chalk" (literally "stones of lime") recalls Moses grinding the gold calf to dust (Exodus 32:20) and Josiah's reform (2 Kings 23:6).

a: the walled city sits alone
p: The deserted city may be the enemy's capital, Samaria, or Jerusalem itself.
b: The "walled city" left for calves to graze is unnamed, like the city of 24:10 and 25:2. Some read it as the oppressor's city, whose fall is the other side of Jacob's forgiveness. Others think of Samaria, destroyed in 722 BC, or of Jerusalem after 587 BC, since the people "with no understanding" (27:11) sounds like Israel (1:3). On that reading, the ruin is the price of the idolatry just described, and mercy comes only after it.

a: its Maker will show it no mercy
p: The same titles that promise comfort elsewhere here bring judgment.
b: God as Israel's "Maker" ('oseh) and "Shaper" (yotser) is a title of tender care in the second half of the book: in 43:1 he is Jacob's "creator" and "the one who shaped you, Israel," who says "Don't be afraid" (43:1; compare 44:2). Here the same titles bring the opposite result: the people's lack of understanding (1:3) closes off mercy. The verb yatsar is the potter's verb, which comes back in 29:16.

a: the LORD will beat out his harvest
p: Threshing with a stick: judgment, or gathering what is precious?
b: Chavat is to beat out grain or olives with a stick, as Ruth "beat out her gleanings" (Ruth 2:17) and Gideon "was beating out wheat" (Judges 6:11). From the Euphrates ("the River") to the Wadi of Egypt are the ideal borders of the promised land (Genesis 15:18; 1 Kings 8:65). The verb can picture judgment, but here the point is gathering: God will collect his people "one by one," like a gleaner picking up every stalk. The Greek has "Rhinocorura," the town at the wadi's mouth (modern El-Arish).

a: the flowing stream of the River
p: The word for "flowing stream" is shibbolet, famous from Judges 12.
b: Shibbolet means both "ear of grain" and "flowing stream." It is the password of Judges 12:6, which the Ephraimites could not pronounce. Here the double meaning suits the harvest picture: God beats out grain "from the shibbolet of the River." The phrase may mean the main channel of the Euphrates, or, as some think, the land's northern edge in general.

a: a great ram's horn will be blown
p: The trumpet of the final gathering: in the daily Jewish prayer and in Jesus' words.
b: The shofar was blown for war, for festivals and for the Jubilee year of release (Leviticus 25:9). "A great shofar" gathering the scattered became a central hope. The daily Amidah prays, "Sound the great shofar for our freedom... and gather us together from the four corners of the earth," and the Rosh Hashanah service reads this verse among its shofar verses. Jesus speaks of the Son of Man sending "his angels out with a great trumpet" to gather his chosen (Matthew 24:31), and Paul of "the trumpet of God" at the resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

a: the strays perishing in the land of Assyria
p: Who are "the lost" in Assyria? Many readers hear the ten northern tribes.
b: Ha'ovdim means "those perishing, those lost," like stray sheep (Jeremiah 50:6; Ezekiel 34:4). Assyria deported the northern tribes in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6), and Judeans fled to Egypt after 587 BC (Jeremiah 43–44). The Talmud cites this verse in its debate over whether the ten tribes will return (Bavli Sanhedrin 110b). Assyria and Egypt here may also stand for the two ends of the whole diaspora. The return ends in worship "on the holy mountain in Jerusalem," where the feast of 25:6 was spread.

a: Woe to the crown
p: Chapters 28–33 are built around six cries of "Woe" (28:1; 29:1; 29:15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1).
b: A new section begins. Chapters 28–33 are arranged around six cries of hoy, "Woe to," the cry of a funeral lament (1 Kings 13:30). Five are aimed at Israel or Judah, and the last at the destroyer (33:1). Most of the material fits the years of the Assyrian threat, especially Hezekiah's revolt against Assyria and his alliance with Egypt (705–701 BC). Unlike chapters 24–27, these oracles name places and groups: Ephraim, Jerusalem's rulers, Ariel, Egypt.

a: Ephraim's drunkards
t: Samaria, the crown on the hill
p: Samaria, capital of northern Israel, sat on a round hill above a fertile valley.
b: Ephraim is the northern kingdom of Israel, and the "crown" set "on the head of a valley thick with fat" is its capital, Samaria, built by Omri on a hill above rich farmland (1 Kings 16:24). Amos had already condemned its wealthy for drinking wine by the bowlful while the poor suffered (Amos 6:1–6). The oracle must come from before Assyria took Samaria in 722 BC. A wilting garland of flowers, worn at drinking parties, is a fitting picture of a city whose glory is already fading. The Greek reads "the hirelings of Ephraim."

a: someone strong and powerful
p: God's strong one is Assyria, pictured as hail, wind and flood.
b: The "strong and powerful" one whom the Lord has ready is Assyria, God's instrument of judgment (10:5). Isaiah pictures its army as a hailstorm and a flood of mighty waters, as he did in 8:7–8, where the king of Assyria is the River overflowing its banks. Shalmaneser V and Sargon II besieged and took Samaria in 724–722 BC (2 Kings 17:5–6; 18:9–10). The same storm and flood images return against Jerusalem in 28:15–19 and against Assyria itself in 30:30.

a: like the first fig of the year
p: Bikkurah: the early fig, so prized that whoever sees it eats it at once.
b: The first figs (bikkurah) ripen in early summer, before the main crop, and were a delicacy (Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1; Jeremiah 24:2). Whoever spots one on the tree picks it and swallows it on the spot. Samaria will be just as quickly devoured. The verb bala', "gulp down, swallow," returns in 28:7, where the priests and prophets "are swallowed up by wine." The drinkers will themselves be swallowed.

a: a crown of beauty
p: The fading crown of the drunkards is replaced by God himself.
b: In 28:1 Ephraim's glory was a crown of fading flowers; now "the LORD of Armies himself" becomes "a crown of beauty and a wreath of splendor" for the remnant. The same words, 'ateret (crown) and tsevi (beauty), are reused. The promise fits the pattern of Isaiah's remnant theology (4:2; 10:20–22), and 62:3 promises that Zion itself will be "a beautiful crown in the LORD's hand" (62:3).

a: these too sway from wine
p: From Samaria the oracle turns to Judah: its religious leaders are drunk as well.
b: "These too" turns the attack from Samaria to Jerusalem. Priest and prophet were meant to give God's instruction (Micah 3:11; Jeremiah 18:18), but they reel from wine and beer as they "see visions" and "give rulings." Priests were forbidden wine while serving (Leviticus 10:9). Whether their drunkenness was literal, at feasts in the Temple, or a picture of spiritual confusion (29:9, "drunk, but not on wine"), the point is that the people's guides cannot guide. The verb "swallowed up" (nivle'u) is a pun on 28:4.

a: Every table is smeared with vomit and filth
p: Qi' tso'ah: a deliberately disgusting picture of the leaders' feasts.
b: Qi' tso'ah, "vomit of filth," is as crude as Hebrew gets. The tables may be the banquet tables of the leaders or even the sacrificial meals at the Temple. The scene is the opposite of the feast on the mountain in 25:6, where God himself serves the finest food and wine. Compare 19:14, where Egypt staggers "the way a drunk wanders in his vomit."

a: Who does he think he is teaching knowledge to?
p: Most read 28:9–10 as the leaders mocking Isaiah's preaching as baby talk.
b: The verse has no speaker marked. Most interpreters hear the drunken priests and prophets mocking Isaiah: "Who does he think we are, babies just weaned?" They treat his message as nursery chatter fit for toddlers (28:10). A few read it as Isaiah's own complaint: whom can God teach, when even the leaders behave like infants? The first reading fits the reply in 28:11–13, where God answers mockery in kind.

a: It is tsav la-tsav
p: Nonsense syllables, alphabet drill, or "precept upon precept"?
b: The line is mostly sounds: tsav la-tsav, tsav la-tsav, qav la-qav, qav la-qav, ze'eir sham, ze'eir sham. Three main readings are offered. (1) Baby talk or gibberish, mocking Isaiah's message. (2) A schoolroom drill: tsade and qof are neighboring letters of the alphabet, chanted by children learning to write. (3) Real words, "command on command, line on line," as the KJV has it: "precept upon precept; line upon line." The Plain English Translation keeps the sounds because the meaning is debated and the sound is the point.
orig: צַו לָצָו צַו לָצָו קַו לָקָו קַו לָקָו

a: a bit here, a bit there!
t: "Line upon line" and its many uses
p: The KJV wording became a proverb for patient teaching.
b: Ze'eir sham means "a little there." In the KJV, "precept upon precept; line upon line; here a little, and there a little," became a familiar phrase for patient, step-by-step teaching, and it is often quoted that way in sermons and in Latter-day Saint scripture (Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 28:30). In context, though, it is the mockers' scorn for Isaiah, and in 28:13 God turns it into judgment. The Greek translator found words in the sounds: "expect affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope, yet a little, yet a little."

a: with jabbering lips and a strange tongue
p: Isaiah means the Assyrians' speech. Paul applies the verse to speaking in tongues.
b: Since the leaders would not hear God in plain Hebrew, they will hear him in the foreign speech of invaders. Deuteronomy had warned of "a nation" from far away: "You will not understand its language" (Deuteronomy 28:49). Paul quotes the verse in 1 Corinthians 14:21: "With other tongues and with the lips of others I will speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me," says the Lord. He uses it to argue that tongues are "a sign for unbelievers" (1 Corinthians 14:22). His wording is closer to Aquila's Greek than to the Septuagint, as Origen noticed.

a: This is where rest is
p: Menuchah: the rest God offered his people in the land.
b: Menuchah, "rest, resting place," is the word for the security God promised Israel in the land: "you have not come to the resting place" (Deuteronomy 12:9), and Solomon praised God for giving "his people Israel a resting place" (1 Kings 8:56). Isaiah's message was simple: give the weary rest, trust God and stop scrambling for alliances (compare 30:15). Jesus' "I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28) and Hebrews 3–4 on the rest that Israel failed to enter take up the same theme.

a: so that they will go and trip backward
p: The five verbs of judgment repeat 8:15.
b: The final line of judgment repeats the verbs of 8:15, where the LORD becomes "a stone that people strike their foot on" and "many will trip... they will fall and break, be trapped and taken captive." The Plain English Translation renders the verbs in the same way in both places. The stone theme of chapter 8 returns three verses later, in the foundation stone of 28:16. The "so that" sounds like purpose, as in the hardening of 6:9–10; many read it as result: the end to which their refusal leads.

a: you men of mockery
p: Lason and moshlei: "scoffers," and a word that means both "rulers" and "makers of proverbs."
b: Anshei latson, "men of scoffing," uses the word for the mocker (lets) of Proverbs, who will not take correction (Proverbs 9:7–8; 13:1). Moshlei means "rulers," but the same letters spell "those who make proverbs" (mashal): perhaps a pun on leaders who coin clever sayings like the one quoted in 28:15. Both groups are "here in Jerusalem," the king's officials who shaped Judah's foreign policy.

a: We have cut a covenant with death
t: What was the covenant with death?
p: A treaty with Egypt, a deal with the god of death, or both?
b: The rulers' boast is probably Isaiah's sarcastic version of their own words. Most think of the treaty with Egypt that Hezekiah's officials made against Assyria around 705–701 BC (30:1–5; 31:1), sealed with oaths before the gods. Since Mot (Death) was a Canaanite god, and Egypt's religion centered on the dead (Osiris), some see a pact made with underworld powers, perhaps by necromancy (8:19; 29:4). Either way, what they called security Isaiah calls a deal with death itself. In 1843 the abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison borrowed the phrase for the U.S. Constitution's protection of slavery: "a covenant with death and an agreement with hell."

a: with Sheol we have signed a pact
p: Chozeh, "pact," is the word for a seer: a deal made by visions?
b: The word translated "pact" is chozeh, which elsewhere means "seer, visionary" (29:10; 30:10). Here it must mean an agreement, but the choice may hint at prophets who "saw" a favorable future for the alliance (28:7, "they sway as they see visions"). Sheol is the world of the dead (5:14; 14:9). The flooding "whip" is a mixed metaphor, a scourge that sweeps like a flood. The written Hebrew has shayit, perhaps an "oar" or a rare spelling of "whip"; the Masoretic reading tradition gives shot, "whip" (compare 10:26).

a: we have made a lie our shelter
p: No one calls their own plan a lie. Isaiah puts God's verdict in their mouths.
b: Real politicians do not say "we have made a lie our shelter." Isaiah gives the rulers' words with God's judgment built in, a technique of prophetic satire. The "shelter" (machseh) is the word for God as refuge in 25:4 and the Psalms (Psalm 46:1); they have put Egypt where God should be. In 28:17 hail and floodwaters wash away the hiding place of lies, as hail and floods destroyed Samaria in 28:2.

a: a cornerstone of great worth, a foundation firmly laid
t: Who or what is the stone?
p: Zion itself, the Davidic king, faith, or the Messiah: the New Testament reads Christ.
b: God sets in Zion a foundation stone, tested and precious, against the rulers' shelter of lies. In Isaiah's setting it may stand for God's promise to Zion and David's house (2 Samuel 7), for the faithful remnant, or for faith itself, the one secure foundation. The Targum makes it a king whom God appoints in Zion, and the Qumran community called its own council "the tested wall, the precious cornerstone" (1QS VIII, 7–8). The New Testament reads Christ: Paul joins this verse with 8:14 (Romans 9:33), and 1 Peter 2:6–8 joins it with 8:14 and Psalm 118:22, "A stone that the builders threw out has become the head of the corner" (Psalm 118:22).
r: 8:14; 2 Samuel 7:16; Psalm 118:22; Romans 9:33; Romans 10:11; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Matthew 21:42

a: a stone that has been tested
p: Bochan may be "tested" or a hard stone used to test metal.
b: 'Even bochan is usually read "a tested stone," from bachan, "test, prove." Some scholars link bochan to an Egyptian word for a hard stone (schist or gneiss) used for building and for testing gold, so "a stone of granite." Either way, it has proven strong. The doubled musad musad, "foundation, founded," stresses that this stone is fixed. In ancient building the cornerstone set the lines for the whole structure; the measuring cord and level of 28:17 continue the picture.

a: Whoever believes will not hurry
t: Not hurry, or not be put to shame?
p: Hebrew: the believer "will not hurry." Greek, quoted in the New Testament: "will not be put to shame."
b: The Hebrew lo' yachish means "will not hurry": the person who trusts does not panic and rush for Egypt (compare 30:15–16, "we will flee on horseback!"). The Greek reads "will not be put to shame," and the New Testament follows it, each writer in his own way. Romans 9:33 joins 28:16 with 8:14 ("I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling") and gives "whoever believes in him will not be put to shame," which is close to the Greek in sense but not word for word. Romans 10:11 quotes the same line and adds "everyone"; Paul's next words depend on it: "there is no difference between Jew and Greek" (Romans 10:12–13). 1 Peter 2:6 follows the Greek in calling the stone "chosen" and precious, and "chosen" has no match in the Hebrew bochan, "tested." The verb he'emin, "believe, trust," recalls 7:9: "If you will not hold firm, you will not be held firm." Some scholars think the last words were meant as the inscription on the stone.

a: I will make justice the measuring cord
p: Qav returns: the line of 28:10 becomes the line of justice.
b: Qav, "measuring line," is the word the mockers chanted as nonsense in 28:10 (qav la-qav). Now God uses it in earnest: justice is the line and righteousness the level (mishqelet, a plumb line or leveling weight) by which the new building is tested. The pair mishpat and tsedaqah, "justice and righteousness," is Isaiah's summary of what God wanted from his vineyard (5:7). What fails the line will be torn down (compare 34:11; 2 Kings 21:13; Amos 7:7–9).

a: Your covenant with death will be wiped out
p: The verb usually means "atone." Here it cancels a treaty.
b: Kuppar is a form of kipper, "atone, cover over," used in 27:9 for Jacob's guilt being atoned for. Here it means "annulled, wiped away": the treaty is cancelled as if it had never been made. Many scholars link it to an older sense "wipe off," known from Akkadian. Judah's covenant with death will not protect it; the "flooding whip" will trample it. The "pact" (chazut) is from the same root as chozeh in 28:15.

a: Just to understand the message will be pure terror
p: Shemu'ah: the "message" the scoffers despised now brings terror.
b: Shemu'ah, "report, message," is the word used in 28:9 by the mockers: "Who is he trying to make understand his message?" Now understanding the message brings only terror, because what it announces has arrived. The same word opens 53:1: "Who has believed what we have heard?" (53:1). Morning after morning the flood returns, a picture of the Assyrian army sweeping through Judah in 701 BC.

a: The bed is short
p: A proverb for a plan that cannot give rest: too short to lie on, too narrow to cover.
b: The verse sounds like a popular proverb: a bed too short to stretch out on, a blanket too narrow to wrap up in. The rulers' alliance with Egypt promised security, but it is like trying to sleep in a bed that does not fit, with a blanket that leaves you cold. It echoes the "rest" they refused in 28:12. The Greek misread the line as "we are pressed and cannot fight."

a: as on Mount Perazim
p: Two of Israel's old victories, now turned against Jerusalem.
b: At Baal-perazim David defeated the Philistines: "The LORD has burst through my enemies ahead of me... the way water bursts through" (2 Samuel 5:20). He then struck them "from Gibeon all the way to Gezer" (1 Chronicles 14:16). In the valley at Gibeon, Joshua's battle ended with hail from the sky: "More died from the hailstones than the Israelites killed with the sword" (Joshua 10:11). Isaiah's hearers knew these as God's victories for Israel. Now God will rise and storm in the same way, but against Jerusalem, a frightening reversal.

a: his deed is strange
p: Judging his own people is "strange" and "foreign" to God. Luther built a theology on it.
b: The words zar ("strange," the word for outsider) and nokhriyyah ("foreign") describe God's act: to fight against his own city is alien to him. Some take this as Isaiah's theology of God's nature: judgment is real, but mercy is his proper work (compare Lamentations 3:33). Martin Luther made the distinction central to his theology: God's "alien work" of humbling and judging serves his "proper work" of forgiving and making alive (Heidelberg Disputation, 1518). Others read the words more simply: what God does will seem unheard of, shocking to those who thought him bound to defend Jerusalem.

a: an end, a settled end
p: Kalah venecheratsah: the same phrase as 10:23, and Daniel 9:27.
b: The phrase kalah venecheratsah, "an end, and decided," repeats 10:23 word for word, where it is the destruction that leaves only a remnant. Daniel 9:27 repeats the pair for the end that God has decreed, and 9:26 and 11:36 echo it. Isaiah claims to have "heard" the decree in the council of the LORD of Armies (compare 6:8; 1 Kings 22:19–22). The warning to stop mocking is the last chance before the bonds grow tighter.

a: Does a farmer plow day after day to plant?
p: God's work, like a farmer's, has seasons and proper measures. Judgment is not forever.
b: The section ends with a wisdom poem. A farmer does not plow forever; he plants each crop in its place, and he threshes each one with the right tool, without crushing it to powder (28:27–28). His skill comes from God (28:26). Many read the parable as an answer to the frightening oracle before it: God's judgment is real, but it is measured and has a purpose, the harvest. Others read it as a defense of Isaiah's message: God's plans, like a farmer's methods, may look strange (28:21) but are wise.

a: black cumin
p: Qetsach is Nigella sativa, small black seeds used as spice; kussemet is emmer or spelt.
b: The crops are real plants of Judah. Qetsach is black cumin (Nigella sativa), a small black seed sprinkled on bread, which is still common in the Middle East. Kammon is cumin. Wheat, barley and kussemet (emmer wheat or spelt) were the main grains (Exodus 9:32). Wheat is set "in rows" and barley "in its marked place," and spelt is planted along the edges. Each crop is placed where it does best. The words sorah and nisman are rare, and their meaning is not certain.

a: His God trains him in the right way to do it
p: Even the farmer's know-how comes from God.
b: Yisserow lammishpat, "he disciplines him in the proper way." The verb is yasar, "train, discipline" (related to musar, 26:16), and mishpat here means "what is right, the proper method." Ancient Near Eastern texts credited the gods with teaching humans agriculture. Isaiah gives that role to the LORD alone, and the wisdom that guides a farmer's season becomes a parable of the wisdom that guides God's own judgments.

a: with a sledge
p: Charuts was a heavy board studded with stones; small seeds were beaten with sticks instead.
b: The charuts was a threshing sledge, a heavy board with sharp stones or iron set into its underside, dragged over the grain by oxen (41:15; Amos 1:3). A cartwheel could also be rolled over grain. But delicate seeds such as black cumin and cumin would be crushed or lost, so they were beaten out with a stick (matteh) or rod (shevet). Both words also mean "staff" or "rod" of punishment (10:5, 10:24). The tool fits the crop, as God's discipline fits his people.

a: He makes his counsel a wonder
p: Pele' and 'etsah: the words of 9:6, and of 25:1.
b: Hifli' 'etsah, "he makes counsel wonderful," uses the two words of the royal name in 9:6, "Wonder-Counselor" (pele' yo'ets). In 25:1 the singer thanked God for "a wonder, plans laid from long ago." Here the farmer's practical wisdom is a small picture of God's great counsel. Tushiyyah, "sound wisdom," is a word of Proverbs and Job (Proverbs 3:21; Job 26:3) for wisdom that works.

a: Woe to Ariel, Ariel
t: Ariel: lion of God, or altar hearth?
p: A code name for Jerusalem. The word can mean "lion of God" or "altar hearth."
b: "Ariel" is a code name for Jerusalem, "the town where David set up camp." The word 'ari'el can be read as "lion of God" (compare 2 Samuel 23:20) or as "altar hearth," the top of the great altar where the sacrifices burned (Ezekiel 43:15–16). The Mesha Stele from Moab (about 840 BC) speaks of an 'r'l, apparently a cult object, which Mesha took from an Israelite town and dragged before his god. The second meaning is the one Isaiah plays on in 29:2: the city will itself become "like an ariel, a fire-altar."

a: the town where David set up camp
p: Chanah, "camp," is also the verb for besieging. David once took the city; now God will.
b: Chanah David may mean "where David encamped," that is, settled (2 Samuel 5:9), or "which David besieged," as the Greek reads it. David captured Jerusalem from the Jebusites (2 Samuel 5:6–9) and made it his capital. In 29:3 God uses the same verb: "I will set my camp all around you." The God who gave David the city will now besiege it. "Let the feasts keep circling" mocks the yearly round of festivals that went on as if nothing could happen (1:13–14).

a: like an ariel, a fire-altar
p: Jerusalem, the city of the altar, will itself become an altar: burning, and drenched in blood.
b: The pun on "Ariel" turns grim. The city where sacrifices burned on the altar hearth will itself become a hearth, where its own people are the offering. Isaiah uses the same image in 30:33 of the fire pit prepared for Assyria, and in 31:9 the LORD is the one "who has a fire in Zion" (31:9). Ezekiel's vision of the slain in the Temple (Ezekiel 9) is a later picture of the same idea: judgment begins at the sanctuary.

a: like the voice of a ghost
p: Ov is a ghost called up by a medium. Jerusalem's voice will be a ghostly whisper.
b: 'Ov is the spirit of a dead person called up by a medium, or the medium's pit itself. In 8:19 Isaiah mocked those who consult the dead, "who chirp and mutter." Saul's medium at Endor saw "a divine being... rising up out of the earth" (1 Samuel 28:13). Here proud Jerusalem is brought so low that its voice will "twitter out of the dust" like a ghost's. The verb tsiftsef, "chirp, twitter," is the bird-like sound people expected from the dead.

a: the horde of outsiders against you
p: Zarayikh: "your outsiders"; the Great Isaiah Scroll has "your arrogant ones."
b: The Hebrew zarayikh is literally "your outsiders," the foreign attackers (compare 25:2, 25:5). (See the variant.) The Great Isaiah Scroll has zedayikh, "your arrogant ones," which differs by one similar letter (r and d look almost the same in Hebrew script), and the Greek has "the ungodly." The attackers will vanish like fine dust and blowing chaff, "suddenly, in a moment."

a: it will happen suddenly, in a moment
p: Many readers see the sudden end of Sennacherib's siege in 701 BC.
b: Verses 1–4 announce a siege; verses 5–8 suddenly turn against the besiegers. Many link the passage with 701 BC, when Sennacherib's army withdrew from Jerusalem (37:36; 2 Kings 19:35, "It happened that night"). Sennacherib's own annals say he shut Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage," but do not claim the city fell. Some scholars think 29:5–8 was added after 701 to turn a threat into a promise; others see judgment and deliverance as one message from the start: God brings Jerusalem to the brink, then rescues it.

a: You will be visited by the LORD of Armies
t: Visited in judgment, or in rescue?
p: Paqad can mean "punish" or "come to help." Is Jerusalem judged or saved?
b: Tippaqed is from paqad, which the Plain English Translation usually renders "call to account" (24:21; 26:21). Here it keeps the older English "visit," because the verb can mean either "punish" or "come to help" (as in Genesis 21:1; Exodus 3:16), and the line can be read both ways. If it continues 29:1–4, Jerusalem is visited with storm and fire. If it begins the turn in 29:5–8, the storm falls on the enemies, and the visit is Jerusalem's rescue. Thunder, earthquake and fire are the signs of God's coming (Exodus 19:16–18; Psalm 18:7–15).

a: As a hungry man dreams
p: The besiegers are like a hungry man who dreams of food and wakes up empty.
b: In 29:7 the nations who attack Ariel become "like a dream." Here the picture is turned around: the attackers themselves are like a hungry or thirsty sleeper who dreams of eating and drinking and wakes with an empty stomach. Their hope of plundering Mount Zion is only a dream. The verse speaks of nefesh, here "belly" and "throat": the craving part of a person.

a: Dawdle and be dumbfounded!
p: Hitmahmehu utemahu, hishta'ash'u vasho'u: commands that sound like what they mean.
b: The verse is built of paired verbs that sound alike: hitmahmehu utemahu, "linger and be astonished," and hishta'ash'u vasho'u, "blind yourselves and be blind." They are ironic commands, like those of 6:9–10: go on, stay blind. "Drunk, but not on wine" picks up the drunken leaders of 28:7. Their stupor is spiritual: they cannot see what God is doing.

a: a spirit of deep sleep
p: The deep sleep that fell on Adam and Abram here falls on the prophets. Paul quotes the Greek.
b: Tardemah is a heavy, God-sent sleep: the sleep of Adam ("the LORD God made a deep sleep fall on the man," Genesis 2:21) and of Abram before the covenant (Genesis 15:12). Here it is a judgment that closes the prophets' eyes. The Greek renders "a spirit of stupor," and Paul joins that phrase with Deuteronomy 29:4: "God gave them a spirit of numbness: eyes that do not see" (Romans 11:8), to explain why many in Israel did not believe the gospel.

a: the prophets
p: "The prophets" and "the visionaries" may be a scribe's notes explaining "eyes" and "heads."
b: The Hebrew reads "he has closed your eyes, the prophets, and covered your heads, the visionaries." Many scholars think "the prophets" and "the visionaries" were added by an early scribe to explain the metaphors, since they sit awkwardly in the line. Others think Isaiah wrote them himself to make the attack on the professional prophets explicit (compare 28:7; 30:10). All the ancient witnesses have them, including the Great Isaiah Scroll, so the Plain English Translation keeps them.

a: like the words of a scroll that is sealed
p: A vision no one can read: sealed for the learned, unreadable for the unlearned.
b: Scrolls were tied and sealed with clay to keep them private or to keep them as legal evidence (Jeremiah 32:10–14). The whole vision is like such a scroll: the educated cannot read it because it is sealed, and the uneducated cannot read at all. Daniel is told to "seal the scroll until the time of the end" (Daniel 12:4), and in Revelation only the Lamb can open the scroll with seven seals (Revelation 5:1–5). Latter-day Saints read 29:11–12 as fulfilled when Martin Harris showed characters from the gold plates to the scholar Charles Anthon in 1828 (Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 27:15–20; Pearl of Great Price, Joseph Smith—History 1:63–65).

a: this people draws near with its mouth
p: Jesus quotes the verse, in the Greek wording, against the traditions of his opponents.
b: The charge is worship without the heart: words and rituals while the heart stays far away. Their "fear" of God has become "a command made by humans and learned by heart." Jesus quotes the verse against the Pharisees' hand-washing traditions: "This people gives me honor with their lips, but their heart keeps far away from me. Their worship of me is empty; the teachings they teach are human commands" (Matthew 15:8–9; compare Mark 7:6–7). His wording follows the Greek, which reads "empty is their worship of me, as they teach human commands and teachings," where the Hebrew speaks of fear learned by rote.

a: a command made by humans and learned by heart
p: Mitsvat 'anashim melummadah: a human command, memorized.
b: Mitsvat 'anashim melummadah is "a commandment of men, taught." The fault is not memorizing in itself, but a fear of God reduced to rules passed on by people and repeated without the heart. Isaiah elsewhere insists that God wants justice and mercy, not just ritual (1:16–17; 58:6–7). The Hebrew word for "taught" is the root of talmid, "student."

a: The wisdom of its wise men will be lost
t: Paul and the wisdom of the wise
p: Paul quotes the verse at 1 Corinthians 1:19 against human wisdom.
b: God answers false worship with "amazing" acts (hafli', the word for "wonder" in 25:1 and 28:29): he will confound the political wise men of Jerusalem whose clever plans left him out (29:15). Paul opens his argument about the cross with this verse: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of those who understand I will set aside" (1 Corinthians 1:19). Paul quotes the Greek, which makes God the subject ("I will destroy") where the Hebrew says the wisdom "will perish" (ve'avedah). He changes only the last verb, the Greek "I will hide," to "I will set aside," perhaps from Psalm 33:10 in the Greek (32:10 there). The cross is God's wonder that confounds the wise.

a: Woe to those who burrow deep
p: The third woe: plans hidden from God, probably the secret negotiations with Egypt.
b: The third woe of chapters 28–33 targets those who "go deep" to hide their plans ('etsah) from the LORD. In Isaiah's setting this is most likely the secret diplomacy with Egypt against Assyria (30:1–2; 31:1), planned without consulting God or his prophet. They say, "Who sees us?" as the wicked do in Psalm 94:7: "Yah does not see." The answer in 29:16 is that the clay cannot hide from the potter.

a: Is the potter to be counted the same as the clay
p: A favorite image of Isaiah and Jeremiah, which Paul uses in Romans 9.
b: Hafkekhem, "your perversity!" or "how you turn things upside down!" To plan in secret is to treat God as if he were the clay and they the potter. The image of God as potter (yotser, the verb of 27:11 and Genesis 2:7) returns in 45:9 and 64:8, and in Jeremiah's visit to the potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6). Paul combines it with 45:9 to answer objections to God's freedom: "Will a shaped thing say to the one who shaped it, 'Why did you make me like this?'" (Romans 9:20).

a: until Lebanon turns into garden land
p: A world turned around: the forest becomes an orchard, and the orchard a forest.
b: Lebanon, famous for its great cedar forests, will become karmel, "garden land, orchard" (also the name of Mount Carmel). The fertile orchard, in turn, will be counted as forest. It is a picture of total reversal, like the proud brought low and the lowly lifted up (29:19–20). In 32:15 the same pair returns when a spirit from on high is poured out, and "the garden land will be thought of as a forest" (32:15).

a: the deaf will hear what a scroll says
p: The sealed scroll of 29:11 will be read, and Jesus points to these signs.
b: In 29:11–12 no one could read the scroll. Now even the deaf hear its words and the blind see out of darkness. The promise of 35:5–6 is similar: "Then blind people's eyes will open" (35:5). Jesus pointed to his healings as these signs when John the Baptist's messengers asked who he was: "The blind see again... and the deaf hear" (Matthew 11:5). The physical and the spiritual meanings run together: the people who were blind to God's work in 29:9–10 will see.

a: The lowly will find more and more joy in the LORD
p: 'Anavim: the humble poor, whose hope is in God.
b: 'Anavim are the humble, the lowly, often also poor and oppressed: people with no power who depend on God. The word is common in the Psalms (Psalm 37:11, where "the humble will take possession of the land"), and Jesus' "Blessed are the gentle, because they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5) uses it in Greek. Their joy is "in the Holy One of Israel," Isaiah's special title for God.

a: who lay snares for the one who calls out wrong in the gate
p: The town gate was the court. The powerful trap anyone who speaks up for justice.
b: In Israelite towns the elders judged cases at the gate (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–2). The mokhiach is one who reproves or argues a case, an honest witness or advocate. Amos says the powerful "hate the one who calls out wrong at the gate" (Amos 5:10). Those who "brand a man guilty with a word" twist testimony, and "empty nothings" (tohu, the word of Genesis 1:2 for formlessness) are false arguments that push the innocent aside. Their end is part of the coming reversal.

a: the LORD, who ransomed Abraham
p: The Bible tells of no ransom of Abraham. Tradition fills the gap.
b: Padah, "ransom, redeem," is the word for buying back a slave or rescuing from danger. The Bible nowhere tells of Abraham's ransom. Most interpreters think of his call out of idolatrous Mesopotamia: "From long ago your ancestors lived on the far side of the River... and they served other gods" (Joshua 24:2). Jewish tradition told that Abraham was thrown into a furnace by Nimrod for refusing to worship idols and was rescued (Genesis Rabbah 38:13), and some Jewish commentators link this verse with that story.
