Some scholars think the phrase was added later, when Abraham had become a model for the returning exiles (51:2).

a: they will treat my name as holy
p: To hallow God's name is to honor him as holy; Jesus' prayer begins with it.
b: Yaqdishu shemi, "they will make my name holy." God's name is already holy; to "hallow" it is to treat it as holy in worship and in life. Jacob's children, "the work of my hands" (compare 60:21), will do what their parents failed to do in 29:13. The Lord's Prayer begins with the same request: "Our Father, who is in heaven, may your name be honored as holy" (Matthew 6:9). "The Holy One of Jacob" appears only here; Isaiah's usual phrase is "the Holy One of Israel."

a: the grumblers will take in teaching
p: The wanderers and grumblers of the wilderness story will finally learn.
b: "Those whose spirits have wandered" and "the grumblers" (rogenim) sound like Israel in the wilderness, who grumbled in their tents (Deuteronomy 1:27; Psalm 106:25). The promise is that they will "take in teaching" (leqach, a word of Proverbs: Proverbs 1:5; 4:2). The section that began with blindness and stupor (29:9–10) ends with understanding. The Greek adds a line: "and the stammering tongues will learn to speak peace" (compare 32:4).

a: Woe to the rebel children
p: Sorerim: the word for the stubborn son of Deuteronomy 21.
b: Banim sorerim, "rebellious children," recalls the law of the "stubborn and rebellious son" (ben sorer) who "will not listen to his father or his mother" (Deuteronomy 21:18). The book opened with the same charge: "Children I have raised and lifted high, and they have rebelled against me" (1:2). The fourth woe of chapters 28–33 is aimed at Judah's leaders, who make plans "that do not come from me." The plan is the alliance with Egypt (30:2), and the phrase "the LORD declares" marks it as God's own charge.

a: who pour out a drink offering my Spirit has no part in
t: A libation, or a woven alliance?
p: Nasakh massekhah: pour a libation to seal a treaty, or weave a web.
b: Linsokh massekhah can mean "to pour a libation," since treaties were sealed with drink offerings to the gods, or "to weave a web," since massekhah also means a woven covering (25:7). Either way, the alliance is made without God's Spirit. The same noun elsewhere means a cast idol (30:22), so some hear a hint that the treaty is a kind of idolatry. Hebrew ruach can be "spirit" or "Spirit"; here God calls it "my Spirit," as in 63:10–11.

a: but have not asked for my word
p: Literally "my mouth they did not ask": the same failure as Joshua's treaty with Gibeon.
b: The Hebrew is "my mouth they did not ask." Kings were expected to "ask" God, through a prophet or priest, before going to war or making treaties (1 Kings 22:5; 1 Samuel 23:2). The most famous failure is Joshua's treaty with the Gibeonites, made because "they did not ask the LORD what to do" (Joshua 9:14). Judah's embassy goes down to Egypt the same way. Deuteronomy 17:16 had forbidden sending the people "back to Egypt to get more horses."

a: find refuge in Egypt's shade
p: Shade is protection. Judah seeks Pharaoh's shade instead of God's.
b: In a hot land, a king's "shade" meant his protection (Judges 9:15; Lamentations 4:20). Psalm 91:1 promises that whoever lives near the Most High "will spend the night in the shadow of the Almighty." Isaiah has just called God "a shade from the heat" for the poor (25:4). Judah's leaders run instead to "Pharaoh's fortress" (ma'oz, the word used for God in 25:4 and 27:5) and "Egypt's shade," which will bring only shame (30:3).

a: his officials are already at Zoan
p: Zoan (Tanis) in the Nile Delta and Hanes, probably Herakleopolis in Middle Egypt.
b: Zoan is Tanis, in the northeastern Nile Delta, a royal city of the period (19:11, 19:13). Hanes is probably Herakleopolis (Egyptian Hnes), in Middle Egypt south of modern Cairo. In Isaiah's time Egypt was ruled by the Kushite (Nubian) 25th Dynasty, and rulers such as Shabaka and Shebitku encouraged revolts against Assyria. "His officials" may be Pharaoh's, showing how far Egypt's power reached, or Judah's king's envoys arriving in Egypt. Egypt's army did come in 701 BC and was defeated at Eltekeh, as Sennacherib reports.

a: The oracle about the animals of the Negev
p: A new oracle title, perhaps taken from its first words, like the riddling headings of chapter 21.
b: Like the headings of 13:1–23:1, this line uses massa', "oracle" (literally a "lifting up" of the voice). It names "the animals of the Negev," the dry south, probably taken from the content of the oracle, as the riddling headings in chapter 21 are (21:1; 21:11; 21:13). The animals may be the dangerous wild beasts of the desert road, or the donkeys and camels carrying Judah's tribute to Egypt. The Greek reads "the vision of the four-footed creatures in the desert."

a: of the viper and the flying burning serpent
p: Saraf me'ofef: the desert's fiery flying snake, as in 14:29.
b: The saraf me'ofef, "flying saraf," appears also in 14:29. Saraf is the "burning" snake whose bite burned (Numbers 21:6, "the burning snakes"), and the same word names the six-winged seraphim of Isaiah's vision (6:2). Egyptian art shows winged cobras as protectors of kings, and the Greek historian Herodotus reports tales of winged serpents in Arabia (Histories 2.75; 3.107). The road through the Negev to Egypt was the land of such terrors, the wilderness Israel once crossed coming out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 8:15).

a: they carry their riches on the shoulders of donkeys
p: Judah's envoys carry treasure across the desert to pay for Egypt's help.
b: The caravan carries Judah's wealth on donkeys and camels across the Negev to buy Egypt's support. The desert route may have been chosen because the coast road was watched by Assyria. Hezekiah would later strip the Temple to pay tribute to Assyria (2 Kings 18:14–16), so this treasure was a costly bet. The irony is that Israel once came out of Egypt through this wilderness with gifts from the Egyptians (Exodus 12:35–36). Now Judah pays to go back.

a: Rahab, who just sits there
p: Rahab is the sea monster, a name for Egypt. Isaiah mocks it as a monster that does nothing.
b: Rahab is the name of a chaos monster defeated by God: "by his skill he struck Rahab down" (Job 26:12; compare Psalm 89:10; 51:9). The name became a nickname for Egypt (Psalm 87:4). The Hebrew rahav hem shavet is literally "Rahab, they, sitting": the dragon that roars but stays seated, all noise and no help. The word rahav also suggests "blustering." Some scholars emend to rahav hammoshbat, "Rahab the silenced," since the text is awkward. Either way, Egypt is a monster defanged.

a: write it down on a tablet in their presence
p: Written oracles stood as evidence: when it came true, everyone would know who said it.
b: Isaiah is told to write the message down, as in 8:1 ("write on it with a common pen") and 8:16 ("Wrap up the witness. Put a seal on the teaching"). A written record could be checked when events came true, showing that God had spoken in advance (compare 41:22–23; 44:7–8). Habakkuk is given a similar order: "Write the vision down, and make it clear on the tablets" (Habakkuk 2:2). The record would stand "for a day yet to come," literally "for the last day," a later time when the people might listen.

a: the teaching of the LORD
p: In Isaiah, torah is the spoken teaching of God through his prophet.
b: Torat YHWH is often rendered "the law of the LORD," but the word torah comes from yarah, "teach, point the way," and in Isaiah it usually means instruction from God through his prophet (1:10; 2:3; 8:16, 8:20). Here it is the message the people refuse to hear, the very words Isaiah has just been told to write down (30:8). The same root gives moreh, "teacher," in 30:20.

a: Talk to us of smooth things
p: The people want prophets who tell them pleasant lies.
b: "Stop seeing!" is what the people want from seers (ro'im) and visionaries (chozim). They want chalaqot, "smooth things," flattering words, and mahatalot, "illusions, fantasies." Amos was told to go home and stop prophesying (Amos 7:12–13), and Micah mocked prophets who promise wine and beer (Micah 2:6, 2:11). The Dead Sea Scrolls call their opponents "the seekers of smooth things" (Damascus Document 1:18; 4QpNah), probably the Pharisees. Paul warns of hearers who want teachers to suit their own desires (2 Timothy 4:3–4).
r: Amos 2:12; Amos 7:12–13; Micah 2:6; Micah 2:11; Jeremiah 5:31; 1 Kings 22:8; 2 Timothy 4:3–4

a: Get the Holy One of Israel out of our sight!
t: The title they wanted to stop hearing
p: Isaiah answers by using the title twice more in the next four verses.
b: "The Holy One of Israel" is Isaiah's signature title for God, used about 25 times in the book and rarely elsewhere. It sums up his vision in the Temple (6:3). The people are tired of it: "Make the Holy One of Israel cease from before us." Isaiah's reply is to begin the next two oracles with it: "So the Holy One of Israel says this" (30:12) and "For the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, says this" (30:15).

a: like a breach in a high wall
p: Their guilt is like a crack in a wall that swells outward and then suddenly collapses.
b: Mud-brick and rubble walls could crack and bulge as water worked into them, until the whole section gave way without warning. Judah's guilt, its trust in "oppression and deviousness" (30:12), is a hidden crack: all seems sound until the moment of collapse. The word for "suddenly, in a moment" (pit'om lefeta') is the phrase used for the enemies' fall in 29:5. Ezekiel 13:10–16 uses a similar image of a wall covered with whitewash.

a: It will be smashed like a potter's jar
p: A jar smashed so fine that not even a fragment remains for carrying coals.
b: Broken pottery was useful: a large shard could carry live coals from a neighbor's fire or scoop water from a cistern. Isaiah pictures a jar smashed so completely that no useful piece is left. Jeremiah would later smash a clay jar before Jerusalem's elders as a sign, saying, "In this way I will break this people and this city" (Jeremiah 19:10–11). The picture connects with the potter and the clay of 29:16 and 45:9.

a: By turning back and resting you will be saved
p: One of Isaiah's best-known lines: is it a call to repentance, or to sit still and not fight?
b: Beshuvah wanachat tiwwashe'un, behashqet uvevitchah tihyeh gevuratkhem: "in returning and rest you will be saved; in quietness and trust will be your strength." Shuvah can mean "repentance" (turning back to God) or "withdrawal" from military plans. Many read it as Isaiah's consistent political advice since 7:4 ("stay quiet. Do not be afraid"): trust God and do not rush into alliances. Others hear a deeper call to repentance and faith, as in 28:12 and 28:16. The verse ends with the saddest words in the chapter: "But you refused."

a: we will flee on horseback!
p: Nanus and al-sus: "we will flee" on "horses", a pun Isaiah turns against them.
b: The people's boast plays on sound: 'al-sus nanus, "on horses we will flee (or speed)." Isaiah turns it around: 'al-ken tenusun, "therefore you will flee." Then 'al-qal nirkav, "on swift ones we will ride," is answered by 'al-ken yiqallu rodfekhem, "therefore your pursuers will be swift." Horses were Egypt's great export, and the alliance promised chariotry (31:1; 36:9). "These have chariots, and those have horses, but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7).

a: One thousand of you will flee at one man's war cry
p: The old promise that a few Israelites would rout many is turned upside down.
b: Leviticus promised that "five of you will chase a hundred" (Leviticus 26:8), and Moses' song asked, "How could one chase a thousand... unless their Rock had sold them off?" (Deuteronomy 32:30). Here the curse of Leviticus 26:36 comes true instead: a thousand Judeans flee from one enemy. What is left of the army will be like a lonely pole on a hilltop, the remnant of a nation that would not trust. In 30:29 God is called "the Rock of Israel."

a: the LORD is waiting to show you favor
p: The people would not wait for God, so God waits for them.
b: Yechakkeh, "he waits," is the same verb as in the last line: "Happy are all who wait (chokhei) for him." The people would not wait for God and ran to Egypt instead; God, for his part, waits to show favor. "He is lifted high" may mean he rises to act, or that he waits on high, at a distance, until the people are ready. "A God of justice" (mishpat) here means a God who does what is right, not one who only punishes. Daniel 12:12 uses the same blessing on those who wait.

a: You will not weep, no, never weep again
p: The promise of 25:8 is applied to Zion.
b: The Hebrew doubles the verb: bakho lo' tivkeh, "weeping you will not weep." The promise of 25:8, that God will "wipe the tears off every face," now comes home to the people of Zion. God will answer "the moment he hears." Isaiah 65:19 repeats the promise for the new Jerusalem: "The sound of weeping and the sound of crying out will no longer be heard there" (65:19).

a: the bread of distress and the water of hardship
p: The prison ration of 1 Kings 22: the hard times will come, but they will not last.
b: The phrase recalls the punishment of the prophet Micaiah, whom King Ahab ordered fed "the bread of hardship and the water of hardship" (1 Kings 22:27). It describes the scarce rations of a siege, such as Jerusalem endured in 701 BC. God does not promise to remove hardship at once. He promises something better within it: the teacher who seemed hidden will be seen.

a: your teacher will not hide in a corner anymore
p: Moreykha may be God himself, the Teacher, or the prophets, "your teachers."
b: Moreykha can be read as singular, "your Teacher," or plural, "your teachers." The verb "hide" is singular in the Masoretic Text, which suggests God himself: the Teacher who seemed hidden (compare 8:17; 45:15) will be seen. The Great Isaiah Scroll has a plural verb, which suggests human teachers, the prophets the people silenced in 30:10. The word is from the root of torah (30:9), and the Qumran community later used moreh tsedeq, "the Teacher of Righteousness," for its leader.

a: This is the road. Walk on it
p: A guide calls from behind whenever the traveler drifts to the right or left.
b: The picture is of a shepherd or guide walking behind, calling out when a traveler drifts off the path. "To the right or to the left" is the language of Deuteronomy: "Do not turn off to the right or to the left" (Deuteronomy 5:32), and Proverbs: "Do not veer off to the right or the left" (Proverbs 4:27). The people who told the prophets to "get off the road" (30:11) will now hear the voice that keeps them on it.

a: like a stained menstrual cloth
p: Idols will be treated as ritually unclean and thrown away.
b: The silver plating and gold covering of idols were valuable, but the people will treat them as unclean. Dawah refers to a menstrual cloth, which was ritually unclean under the Law (Leviticus 15:19–24). Ezekiel uses the same word for silver and gold thrown into the streets (Ezekiel 7:19–20). The cry "Out!" (tse') is the word used to drive away something defiling. The turn from idols follows the turn back to the teacher in 30:20–21.

a: will eat salted feed
p: Chamits: fodder seasoned with salt or sorrel, food fit for people.
b: Belil chamits is "seasoned fodder," mixed with salt or with sour herbs (sorrel), and winnowed clean of chaff with a shovel and fork. Ordinary oxen and donkeys will eat feed as good as people's food. The abundance of 30:23–26 recalls the blessings promised for obedience (Deuteronomy 28:11–12) and anticipates the new creation's peace among animals (11:6–9; 65:25).

a: when the towers fall
t: The day of the great slaughter
p: Streams flow on the mountains on the same day that proud towers fall.
b: "The day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall" sets the blessing against the background of judgment, as in 2:15, where the day of the LORD comes "against every tall tower." The towers may be the fortifications of the enemy or the proud defenses of Judah itself. Streams on every hill turn the dry land of the Negev (30:6) into a well-watered garden, a promise that grows in chapters 35 and 41 (35:6–7; 41:18).

a: the sun's light will be seven times as strong
p: A picture of the age of healing. The rabbis debated whether it refers to the messianic age or the world to come.
b: The moon will shine like the sun, and the sun seven times as bright, "like the light of seven days," perhaps the light of the seven days of creation gathered into one. Rabbi Hisda set this verse beside 24:23, where sun and moon are ashamed, and explained that one speaks of the days of the Messiah and the other of the world to come (Bavli Sanhedrin 91b). Revelation goes further: the city "does not need the sun or the moon" (Revelation 21:23; compare Isaiah 60:19–20). The light comes on the day God "bandages" and "heals" his people (Psalm 147:3; 61:1).

a: The name of the LORD is coming from far away
p: God's "name" stands for God himself, present and active.
b: In Deuteronomy, God makes "his name" dwell in the place he chooses (Deuteronomy 12:5, 12:11). Here the name itself comes "from far away" like a storm, with burning anger, thick smoke, lips of rage, and a tongue like fire. The picture is of a theophany, God's coming in power, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:18) and in the storm psalms (Psalm 18:7–15; Psalm 29). The coming is against Assyria (30:31) and brings deliverance for Zion.

a: to shake the nations in a sieve of nothingness
p: The nations are sifted to nothing and led away with a bridle, like animals.
b: Two pictures follow the flood of God's breath. The nations are shaken in a sieve, but the sieve is "of nothingness" (shav'): nothing will be left. Then a bridle (resen) is put in their jaws, but it "leads them astray," into destruction. In 37:29 God tells Sennacherib, "I will put my hook in your nose and my bridle on your lips." The flood that reaches "up to the neck" recalls 8:8, where Assyria itself was the flood.

a: like the night when a festival is made holy
p: The festival kept at night is most likely Passover, the feast of rescue from Egypt.
b: Most of Israel's festivals began in the daytime, but Passover was a night feast: "a night of keeping watch for the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt" (Exodus 12:42). Judah, which tried to find safety in Egypt, will instead sing like those who celebrated rescue from Egypt. Pilgrims went up to Jerusalem with the flute (Psalm 42:4; 1 Samuel 10:5). Many have linked this with the night Sennacherib's army was struck (37:36), in the spirit of the Passover destroyer.

a: with the rod he will strike
p: Assyria, God's rod, is now struck with the rod.
b: In 10:5 the LORD said, "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger!" and called it a stick that carried his rage. Now Assyria itself is shattered by the voice of the LORD and beaten with the rod. The farmer's "rod" (shevet) of 28:27 and the "staff" of 30:32 continue the picture. Judah will hear the blows as music: tambourines and lyres (30:32), like the singers whose praise preceded victory in 2 Chronicles 20:21–22.

a: Every stroke of the destined staff
p: Matteh musadah: a staff "appointed" or "founded," or by a small change, "of discipline."
b: Matteh musadah is literally "a staff of foundation," probably "appointed, destined" staff. Many scholars read mussarah, "of discipline," by a small change, which fits the punishment picture; the Great Isaiah Scroll's form also differs. At the end of the verse, the written Hebrew has "against her" and the Masoretic reading tradition "against them"; the Plain English Translation follows the Qere. The scene is a ritual of victory: blows fall on Assyria while Judah keeps time with tambourines.

a: For Topheth was laid out long ago
p: Topheth was the place of child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom: the root of "Gehenna."
b: Topheth was in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, on the south side of Jerusalem, where children were burned as offerings. Josiah "made unclean" Topheth, "so that no one would ever again make his son or his daughter pass through the fire for Molech" (2 Kings 23:10; compare Jeremiah 7:31–32). It "has been made ready for the king" (lammelekh), a likely pun on Molech: the king of Assyria will be burned in it. The Valley of Hinnom, Ge-Hinnom, became the name "Gehenna" for the place of final judgment in later Jewish and Christian thought.

a: like a stream of sulfur
p: The breath of God sets the pit alight like a stream of sulfur.
b: Sulfur (brimstone) and fire destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah: "the LORD rained sulfur and fire" (Genesis 19:24). In Isaiah 34:9 Edom's streams turn to pitch and its soil to sulfur. Revelation takes up the picture for the final judgment: the beast and the false prophet are "thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur" (Revelation 19:20), and the devil follows (Revelation 20:10). The "breath of the LORD" that brings life (Genesis 2:7) here brings destruction.
